claim: SDH inhibition impairs cell proliferation in 143B cells cultured in media without electron acceptors.
source: Both inhibitors effectively blocked cell proliferation when cultured in media without electron acceptors (DMEM without pyruvate), consistent with an essential role of mitochondrial metabolism in support of cell proliferation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A measuring proliferation rates under different treatment conditions.

claim: Pyruvate and alpha-ketobutyrate robustly restore proliferation upon rotenone treatment.
source: While we confirm that PYR and AKB can robustly restore proliferation upon rotenone treatment, proliferation of AA5 treated cells was only modestly improved by electron acceptor supplementation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental proliferation data shown in Figure 1A comparing effects of PYR and AKB on rotenone vs AA5 treated cells.

claim: Proliferation of AA5 treated cells is only modestly improved by electron acceptor supplementation.
source: While we confirm that PYR and AKB can robustly restore proliferation upon rotenone treatment, proliferation of AA5 treated cells was only modestly improved by electron acceptor supplementation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental proliferation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Aspartate supplementation equivalently restores cell proliferation to both rotenone and AA5-treated cells.
source: In contrast, aspartate supplementation equivalently, albeit incompletely, restored cell proliferation to both rotenone and AA5-treated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental proliferation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Aspartate is poorly permeable to most cells even at supraphysiological concentrations.
source: Aspartate is poorly permeable to most cells even at supraphysiological concentrations, so we generated 143B cells expressing the glial-specific aspartate transporter SLC1A3, which we confirm supports aspartate uptake at micromolar extracellular concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2018; Sullivan et al., 2018) and experimental data showing SLC1A3 expression enables aspartate uptake.

claim: SLC1A3 expression supports aspartate uptake at micromolar extracellular concentrations.
source: Aspartate is poorly permeable to most cells even at supraphysiological concentrations, so we generated 143B cells expressing the glial-specific aspartate transporter SLC1A3, which we confirm supports aspartate uptake at micromolar extracellular concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C measuring aspartate uptake.

claim: Improved aspartate uptake with SLC1A3 expression allows aspartate to fully restore proliferation upon AA5 treatment.
source: Notably, improved aspartate uptake with SLC1A3 expression allowed aspartate to fully restore proliferation upon AA5 treatment, regardless of PYR co-treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental proliferation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Intracellular expression of guinea pig asparaginase combined with asparagine treatment restores proliferation to AA5-treated cells.
source: Similarly, orthogonal aspartate acquisition by intracellular expression of the guinea pig asparaginase (gpASNase1) combined with asparagine treatment was also able to restore proliferation to AA5-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G; Sullivan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G and citation to Sullivan et al., 2018.

claim: Aspartate is a primary metabolic limitation of SDH-impaired cells.
source: These data indicate that aspartate is a primary metabolic limitation of SDH-impaired cells, consistent with previous findings (Cardaci et al., 2015; Lussey-Lepoutre et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by citations to Cardaci et al., 2015 and Lussey-Lepoutre et al., 2015.

claim: The metabolic determinants of aspartate limitation upon SDH inhibition are distinct from those of CI loss.
source: However, these data also indicate that the metabolic determinants of aspartate limitation upon SDH inhibition are distinct from those of CI loss.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing effects of SDH vs CI inhibition.

claim: AA5 treatment causes succinate accumulation.
source: As expected for SDH impairment, AA5 treatment caused succinate accumulation and depleted fumarate levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: AA5 treatment depletes fumarate levels.
source: As expected for SDH impairment, AA5 treatment caused succinate accumulation and depleted fumarate levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Aspartate levels are depleted by both rotenone and AA5 treatment.
source: Consistent with aspartate being the mediator of proliferation defects from either inhibitor, aspartate levels were depleted by both drugs, fully restored by pyruvate in rotenone treated cells, and only partially increased in cells treated with AA5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pyruvate fully restores aspartate levels in rotenone treated cells.
source: Consistent with aspartate being the mediator of proliferation defects from either inhibitor, aspartate levels were depleted by both drugs, fully restored by pyruvate in rotenone treated cells, and only partially increased in cells treated with AA5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pyruvate only partially increases aspartate levels in cells treated with AA5.
source: Consistent with aspartate being the mediator of proliferation defects from either inhibitor, aspartate levels were depleted by both drugs, fully restored by pyruvate in rotenone treated cells, and only partially increased in cells treated with AA5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The correlation between proliferation rate and aspartate levels is consistent across inhibitors and environmental conditions, manifesting as a hyperbolic relationship.
source: Notably, combining these datasets revealed that the correlation between proliferation rate and aspartate levels was consistent across inhibitors and environmental conditions, manifesting as a hyperbolic relationship (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by combined analysis of proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AA5 treatment is not associated with suppression of NAD+/NADH.
source: Unlike with rotenone treatment, AA5 treatment was not associated with suppression of NAD+/NADH, breaking the direct correlation between NAD+/NADH, aspartate levels, and proliferation rate seen with rotenone and other CI inhibitors (Figure 1D; Gui et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1D and citation to Gui et al., 2016.

claim: Pyruvate supplementation increases NAD+/NADH in all treatment conditions.
source: Pyruvate supplementation increased NAD+/NADH in all cases; restoring NAD+/NADH in rotenone treated cells to near vehicle-treated levels and increasing NAD+/NADH beyond vehicle treated cells upon AA5 treatment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CI impairments suppress aspartate production by lowering NAD+/NADH and thereby slowing the oxidative TCA cycle.
source: These data are consistent with a model where CI impairments suppress aspartate production by lowering NAD+/NADH and thereby slowing the oxidative TCA cycle, whereas SDH inhibition directly blocks the oxidative TCA cycle, impairing aspartate synthesis and NADH production (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by model shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SDH inhibition directly blocks the oxidative TCA cycle, impairing aspartate synthesis and NADH production.
source: These data are consistent with a model where CI impairments suppress aspartate production by lowering NAD+/NADH and thereby slowing the oxidative TCA cycle, whereas SDH inhibition directly blocks the oxidative TCA cycle, impairing aspartate synthesis and NADH production (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by model shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pyruvate treatment restores metabolic progression through the TCA cycle in rotenone-treated cells but not in cells treated with AA5.
source: Indeed, we measured M+4 aspartate in cells cultured in U-13C glutamine, reflective of aspartate produced via canonical oxidative TCA cycle activity and found that pyruvate treatment restores metabolic progression through the TCA cycle in rotenone-treated cells but not in cells treated with AA5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Re-expression of wild type SDHB in UOK269 cells alleviates the accumulation of succinate.
source: Re-expression of wild type SDHB in UOK269 cells had the expected metabolic effects by alleviating the accumulation of succinate and increasing aspartate levels (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1M and N).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M.

claim: Re-expression of wild type SDHB in UOK269 cells increases aspartate levels.
source: Re-expression of wild type SDHB in UOK269 cells had the expected metabolic effects by alleviating the accumulation of succinate and increasing aspartate levels (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1M and N).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claim: An intact TCA cycle ameliorates the dependence of UOK269 cells on pyruvate or aspartate for cell proliferation.
source: Similar to 143B cells, an intact TCA cycle ameliorated the dependence of UOK269 cells on pyruvate or aspartate for cell proliferation (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In UOK269 cells, pyruvate and aspartate treatment are equally effective at restoring cell proliferation.
source: However, in contrast to AA5 treated 143B cells, pyruvate and aspartate treatment were equally effective at restoring cell proliferation in UOK269 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Long-term SDH loss may be associated with metabolic adaptations that allow cells to fully take advantage of exogenous electron acceptors to restore aspartate and cell proliferation.
source: These data suggest that long-term SDH loss may be associated with metabolic adaptations that allow cells to fully take advantage of exogenous electron acceptors to restore aspartate and cell proliferation.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing acute vs chronic SDH loss.

claim: Treatment with AA5 only partially impairs respiration after several hours of treatment.
source: In support of this, we found that treatment with AA5 only partially impairs respiration after several hours of treatment, whereas rotenone severely abrogates respiration within minutes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rotenone severely abrogates respiration within minutes.
source: In support of this, we found that treatment with AA5 only partially impairs respiration after several hours of treatment, whereas rotenone severely abrogates respiration within minutes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SDH-mutant cancer cells manifest with decreased CI expression and activity.
source: One potential explanation for the respiration loss in SDH-mutant cells is the observation that they manifest with decreased CI expression and activity (Cardaci et al., 2015; Lorendeau et al., 2017; Saxena et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cardaci et al., 2015; Lorendeau et al., 2017; Saxena et al., 2016.

claim: Dual inhibition of SDH and CI is required to mimic the metabolic phenotype of SDH-mutant cancer cells.
source: Indeed, it was reported that dual inhibition of SDH and CI is required to mimic the metabolic phenotype of SDH-mutant cancer cells (Lorendeau et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorendeau et al., 2017.

claim: CI inhibition causes a robust restoration of cell proliferation in SDH-impaired cells in the presence of electron acceptors.
source: We tested if, in the presence of electron acceptors, rotenone could alter the proliferation of cells treated with AA5 and, surprisingly, found it caused a robust restoration of cell proliferation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CI co-inhibition partially restores aspartate to SDH-impaired cells to a level consistent with their improved proliferation rate.
source: Since aspartate levels define the proliferation rate of SDH-impaired cells, we then measured aspartate levels and found that CI co-inhibition partially restored aspartate to SDH-impaired cells to a level consistent with their improved proliferation rate (Figure 1C, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2B and correlation analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: CI co-inhibition restores proliferation and increases aspartate levels across a panel of diverse human cell lines treated with AA5.
source: CI co-inhibition also restored proliferation and increased aspartate levels across a panel of diverse human cell lines treated with AA5, including both transformed (A549, HCT116) and non-transformed (293T, TF-1) cells, indicating that this metabolic relationship was generalizable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: CI inhibition is sufficient for successful generation of SDHB KO clones from Cas9/sgSDHB nucleofected 143B cells.
source: Based on our previous observations, we repeated colony selection with or without rotenone and found that CI inhibition was sufficient for successful generation of clones from Cas9/sgSDHB nucleofected 143B cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by clone generation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Every tested clone generated in the presence of rotenone was devoid of SDHB expression.
source: Notably, every tested clone generated in this manner was devoid of SDHB expression (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AA5 treatment of an SDHB KO clone has no significant effects on proliferation, aspartate levels or the NAD+/NADH ratio.
source: We also found that AA5 treatment of an SDHB KO clone had no significant effects on proliferation, aspartate levels or the NAD+/NADH ratio, indicating on-target effects of AA5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In SDHB KO cell lines, proliferation is improved by treatment with CI inhibitors rotenone or metformin, or by supplementation with aspartate.
source: In each SDHB KO cell line generated, proliferation was slowed relative to their parental cells but was improved by treatment with the CI inhibitors rotenone or metformin, or by supplementation with aspartate (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Restoration of SDHB expression in a KO clone rescues proliferation to parental rates.
source: We also restored SDHB expression in a KO clone and found that it rescued proliferation to parental rates and reinstated wild type relationships with rotenone and AA5 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: Rotenone decreases aspartate levels in WT cells but increases aspartate in SDHB KO cells.
source: We then measured aspartate levels in WT and SDHB KO cells with or without rotenone treatment and found that rotenone decreases aspartate levels in WT cells but increases aspartate in SDHB KO cells, consistent with proliferation restoration (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: AA5 impairs cell proliferation in HPLM and rotenone or aspartate co-treatment restores cell proliferation.
source: We found that AA5 still impaired cell proliferation and that rotenone or aspartate co-treatment restored cell proliferation in HPLM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: CI inhibition is sufficient to induce aspartate levels and cell proliferation in diverse cell lines and media conditions upon SDH disruption.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that CI inhibition is sufficient to induce aspartate levels and cell proliferation in diverse cell lines and media conditions upon SDH disruption.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental datasets across different cell lines and media conditions.

claim: Treatment with antimycin or oligomycin can substitute for CI inhibitors to restore the proliferation and aspartate levels of AA5 treated cells.
source: Importantly, we found that treatment with antimycin or oligomycin can substitute for CI inhibitors, albeit less effectively, to restore the proliferation and aspartate levels of AA5 treated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Complex III inhibition with antimycin treatment has near identical effects on aspartate levels and proliferation as AA5 and rotenone cotreatment.
source: Gratifyingly, since complex III inhibition collaterally impairs both complex I and II, antimycin treatment alone had near identical effects on aspartate levels and proliferation as AA5 and rotenone cotreatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Culturing cells in severe hypoxia (1%) is sufficient to improve the proliferation of SDH-impaired cells.
source: Finally, culturing cells in severe hypoxia (1%) was sufficient to improve the proliferation of SDH-impaired cells, albeit to a smaller degree than CI inhibition, while physiological O2 tensions (3–11%) had little effect on the proliferation of AA5 treated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The shared effect of ETC inhibition treatments on mitochondrial NAD+/NADH is likely a primary mechanism by which ETC inhibition supports aspartate production and proliferation in SDH-deficient cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the shared effect of each treatment on mitochondrial NAD+/NADH, rather than other downstream effects on ETC function, is likely a primary mechanism by which ETC inhibition supports aspartate production and proliferation in SDH-deficient cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing multiple ETC inhibitors.

claim: AA5 treatment increases NAD+/NADH in the presence of pyruvate.
source: While AA5 treatment alone increased NAD+/NADH in the presence of pyruvate, as in Figure 1D, the effects of rotenone co-treatment were epistatic to AA5 treatment and reduced cellular NAD+/NADH to that of cells treated with rotenone alone (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Rotenone co-treatment reduces cellular NAD+/NADH to that of cells treated with rotenone alone.
source: While AA5 treatment alone increased NAD+/NADH in the presence of pyruvate, as in Figure 1D, the effects of rotenone co-treatment were epistatic to AA5 treatment and reduced cellular NAD+/NADH to that of cells treated with rotenone alone (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in NAD+/NADH in cells upon SDH impairment alone is likely a consequence of decreased NADH production in the TCA cycle coinciding with persisting NADH oxidation by active mitochondrial CI.
source: The increase in NAD+/NADH in cells upon SDH impairment alone is thus likely a consequence of decreased NADH production in the TCA cycle coinciding with persisting NADH oxidation by active mitochondrial CI.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on NAD+/NADH measurements.

claim: Mitochondrial NAD+/NADH is lower than cytosolic NAD+/NADH in vehicle-treated conditions.
source: As expected, in vehicle-treated conditions, mitochondrial NAD+/NADH was lower than cytosolic NAD+/NADH (Figure 3B; Williamson et al., 1967).
evidence: Supported by compartmentalized NAD+/NADH measurements shown in Figure 3B and citation to Williamson et al., 1967.

claim: The effects on NAD+/NADH from rotenone and/or AA5 treatment are predominantly observed at their site of action in the mitochondria.
source: In addition, the effects on NAD+/NADH from rotenone and/or AA5 treatment were predominantly observed at their site of action in the mitochondria (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by compartmentalized NAD+/NADH measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The absence of changes to cytosolic NAD+/NADH upon mitochondrial inhibitor treatments is expected due to exogenous pyruvate pinning cytosolic NAD+/NADH through lactate dehydrogenase activity.
source: Notably, the absence of changes to cytosolic NAD+/NADH upon mitochondrial inhibitor treatments is expected in this context due to exogenous pyruvate pinning cytosolic NAD+/NADH through lactate dehydrogenase activity.
evidence: Inference based on established knowledge of lactate dehydrogenase function.

claim: MitoLbNOX expression impedes the restorative effect of rotenone treatment on SDH-impaired cell proliferation.
source: Indeed, whereas cells expressing cytoLbNOX behaved similarly to parental cells expressing eGFP, mitoLbNOX expression impeded the restorative effect of rotenone treatment on SDH-impaired cell proliferation (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The increase in aspartate levels upon rotenone co-treatment is diminished by mitoLbNOX expression, but not by cytoLbNOX expression.
source: Moreover, the increase in aspartate levels upon rotenone co-treatment was similarly diminished by mitoLbNOX expression, but not by cytoLbNOX expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Decreased mitochondrial NAD+/NADH is required for the benefits of CI inhibition when SDH is impaired.
source: These data indicate that decreased mitochondrial NAD+/NADH is required for the benefits of CI inhibition when SDH is impaired.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with mitoLbNOX and cytoLbNOX.

claim: AZD7545 treatment slightly improves cell proliferation and increases aspartate levels in AA5-treated cells.
source: Importantly, treatment with AZD7545 also slightly improved cell proliferation and increased aspartate levels in AA5-treated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Compartment-specific mitochondrial redox alterations are both sufficient and required to reprogram aspartate synthesis in SDH-impaired cells.
source: Nonetheless, these data provide additional support that compartment-specific mitochondrial redox alterations are both sufficient and required to reprogram aspartate synthesis in SDH-impaired cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with AZD7545 and LbNOX constructs.

claim: SDHB KO decreases total aspartate levels and abolishes oxidative M+4 aspartate production.
source: SDHB KO decreased total aspartate levels and abolished oxidative M+4 aspartate production, as expected, and RCQ-derived M+3 aspartate was slightly increased in SDHB KO cells upon rotenone treatment (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RCQ-derived M+3 aspartate is slightly increased in SDHB KO cells upon rotenone treatment.
source: SDHB KO decreased total aspartate levels and abolished oxidative M+4 aspartate production, as expected, and RCQ-derived M+3 aspartate was slightly increased in SDHB KO cells upon rotenone treatment (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BMS-303141 has an anti-proliferative effect on AA5 and rotenone co-treated cells, which can be prevented by aspartate supplementation.
source: Indeed, BMS had an anti-proliferative effect on AA5 and rotenone co-treated cells, which could be prevented by aspartate supplementation (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Aspartate levels are decreased in SDH/CI inhibited cells when treated with BMS-303141.
source: Correspondingly, aspartate levels were decreased in SDH/CI inhibited cells when treated with BMS, tracking with the small contribution of RCQ to aspartate production in this context (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RCQ is partially responsible for increased aspartate synthesis and cell proliferation upon CI inhibition in SDH-impaired cells.
source: These data indicate that RCQ is partially responsible for increased aspartate synthesis and cell proliferation upon CI inhibition in SDH-impaired cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with BMS-303141 treatment.

claim: The majority of aspartate in vehicle-treated SDHB KO cells is labeled M+3 from glucose.
source: While glucose-derived carbon was a minor contributor to aspartate in WT cells, the majority of aspartate in vehicle-treated SDHB KO cells was labeled M+3 from glucose, as was most of the aspartate induced by rotenone treatment (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Most of the aspartate induced by rotenone treatment in SDHB KO cells is labeled M+3 from glucose.
source: While glucose-derived carbon was a minor contributor to aspartate in WT cells, the majority of aspartate in vehicle-treated SDHB KO cells was labeled M+3 from glucose, as was most of the aspartate induced by rotenone treatment (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PC KO cells are sensitive to SDH impairment.
source: Consistent with previously published results, we find that PC KO cells are sensitive to SDH impairment (Figure 4H; Cardaci et al., 2015; Lussey-Lepoutre et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 4H and citations to Cardaci et al., 2015 and Lussey-Lepoutre et al., 2015.

claim: Rotenone treatment provides a proliferative benefit to AA5-treated PC KO cells.
source: Interestingly, rotenone treatment still provided a proliferative benefit to AA5-treated PC KO cells, although the resultant proliferation rate was still decreased compared to PC AB cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: BMS treatment completely blocks cell proliferation in SDH/CI inhibited PC KO cells and is ameliorated by aspartate treatment.
source: We hypothesized that this residual proliferation benefit was driven by existing or compensatory RCQ activity, so we added BMS to SDH/CI inhibited PC KO cells, which was sufficient to completely block cell proliferation and was ameliorated by aspartate treatment (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: BMS treatment blocks the increase in aspartate levels upon rotenone treatment in SDH-impaired PC KO cells.
source: Consistent with the proliferation defects, BMS treatment also blocked the increase in aspartate levels upon rotenone treatment in SDH-impaired PC KO cells (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Both alternative aspartate synthesis pathways, RCQ and PC, contribute to aspartate levels and cell proliferation during SDH deficiency and are activated by CI impairment.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that both alternative aspartate synthesis pathways, RCQ and PC, contribute to aspartate levels and cell proliferation during SDH deficiency and are activated by CI impairment (Figure 4J).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with PC KO and BMS treatment.

claim: Proliferation of MPC1 KO cells is completely ablated by SDH impairment and no longer improved by CI co-inhibition.
source: Proliferation of MPC1 KO cells was moderately decreased in vehicle-treated conditions, but completely ablated by SDH impairment and no longer improved by CI co-inhibition, while MPC1 AB control cells mirrored WT cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Aspartate levels are decreased by AA5 treatment in MPC1 KO cells and are not restored during rotenone cotreatment.
source: Consistent with MPC activity supporting the alternative aspartate synthesis pathways induced by CI inhibition in SDH-impaired cells, we found that aspartate levels were decreased by AA5 treatment in MPC1 KO cells and were not restored during rotenone cotreatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Aspartate supplementation rescues proliferation in SDH-impaired MPC1 KO cells during both SDH inhibition and SDH/CI co-inhibition.
source: To confirm that the proliferation defects in SDH-impaired MPC1 KO cells were mediated by aspartate depletion, we supplemented MPC1 KO cells with aspartate, and observed robust proliferation rescues during both SDH inhibition and SDH/CI co-inhibition (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mitochondrial pyruvate import is a critical component of alternative aspartate synthesis pathways in SDH-impaired cells.
source: Thus, mitochondrial pyruvate import is a critical component of alternative aspartate synthesis pathways in SDH-impaired cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with MPC1 KO cells.

claim: MPC1 KO is associated with a depletion in AKG.
source: We noted that MPC1 KO was associated with a depletion in AKG, suggesting that mitochondrial pyruvate entry may support RCQ by driving AKG generation (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The requirement for MPC1 to maintain AKG levels suggests that pyruvate-dependent GPT2 activity is a dominant route for AKG production in these cells.
source: The requirement for MPC1 to maintain AKG levels suggests that pyruvate-dependent GPT2 activity is a dominant route for AKG production in these cells, consistent with recent studies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Rossiter et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Weinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by citations to Rossiter et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022; Weinberg et al., 2010.

claim: MPC1 KO is associated with a decrease in alanine levels.
source: Indeed, MPC1 KO was also associated with a decrease in alanine levels, corroborating studies that identify GPT2 as a dominant source of alanine production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Rossiter et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to Rossiter et al., 2021.

claim: Rotenone co-treatment is associated with further depletion of AKG in MPC1 KO cells.
source: While AA5 treatment did not alter AKG levels in MPC1 KO cells, the addition of rotenone co-treatment was associated with further depletion of AKG, but not alanine, suggesting that rotenone blocked the secondary path of AKG generation through redox changes that impair the NAD +consuming GDH reaction (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A reduced mitochondrial environment promotes alternative aspartate synthesis in SDH-deficient cells through activating RCQ and PC activity, both of which require mitochondrial pyruvate import.
source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that a reduced mitochondrial environment promotes alternative aspartate synthesis in SDH-deficient cells through activating RCQ and PC activity, both of which require mitochondrial pyruvate import (Figure 5F).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with MPC1 KO cells.

claim: GOT2 KO cells are unable to proliferate in pyruvate-free media.
source: Consistent with published phenotypes, GOT2 KO cells were unable to proliferate in pyruvate-free media (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2022; Kerk et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations to Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2022 and Kerk et al., 2022.

claim: GOT2 KO cells have increased sensitivity to SDH inhibition alone but maintain the benefits of CI co-inhibition on proliferation rate and aspartate production.
source: In our standard media containing pyruvate, we found that GOT2 KO cells have increased sensitivity to SDH inhibition alone but maintained the benefits of CI co-inhibition on proliferation rate and aspartate production, similar to GOT2 AB and WT cells (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Aspartate supplementation phenocopies the proliferation benefits of rotenone co-treatment in GOT2 KO cells.
source: The enhanced depletion of aspartate upon AA5 treatment in GOT2 KO cells was also functionally related to its stronger proliferation impairment phenotype, as aspartate supplementation was able to phenocopy the proliferation benefits of rotenone co-treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Residual aspartate production in SDH-impaired cells is primarily driven by GOT2.
source: These data indicate that residual aspartate production in SDH-impaired cells is primarily driven by GOT2, but GOT2 is dispensable for the induction of aspartate production in SDH-impaired cells upon CI inhibition.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with GOT2 KO cells.

claim: GOT2 is dispensable for the induction of aspartate production in SDH-impaired cells upon CI inhibition.
source: These data indicate that residual aspartate production in SDH-impaired cells is primarily driven by GOT2, but GOT2 is dispensable for the induction of aspartate production in SDH-impaired cells upon CI inhibition.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with GOT2 KO cells.

claim: CI inhibition no longer provides a proliferative benefit in SDH-impaired GOT1 KO cells.
source: Importantly, SDH-impaired GOT1 KO cells differed from GOT1 AB and WT cells in that CI inhibition no longer provided a proliferative benefit (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: CI co-inhibition only increases aspartate levels in GOT1 replete cells.
source: Correspondingly, aspartate levels were suppressed by SDH impairment in both GOT1 KO and GOT1 AB cell lines, but CI co-inhibition only increased aspartate levels in GOT1 replete cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: CI inhibition still increases malate levels in SDH-impaired GOT1 KO cells.
source: Notably, CI inhibition still increased malate levels in SDH-impaired GOT1 KO cells, suggesting that the mitochondrial redox changes from CI inhibition still drive the biochemical pathways required for alternative aspartate synthesis in these cells (i.e. PC and RCQ), but that GOT1 is required for terminal aspartate generation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GOT1 is required for terminal aspartate generation in SDH/CI impaired cells.
source: Notably, CI inhibition still increased malate levels in SDH-impaired GOT1 KO cells, suggesting that the mitochondrial redox changes from CI inhibition still drive the biochemical pathways required for alternative aspartate synthesis in these cells (i.e. PC and RCQ), but that GOT1 is required for terminal aspartate generation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with GOT1 KO cells.

claim: Neither proliferation rate nor aspartate levels are restored by CI inhibition in SDH-impaired MDH1 KO cells.
source: Similar to GOT1 KO cells, we found that neither proliferation rate nor aspartate levels were restored by CI inhibition in SDH-impaired MDH1 KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Baseline aspartate levels are elevated in both GOT1 KO and MDH1 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, baseline aspartate levels were elevated in both GOT1 KO and MDH1 KO cells, consistent with their conventional aspartate-consuming role in the malate-aspartate shuttle (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: GOT1 KO or MDH1 KO prevents CI inhibition from restoring aspartate levels in SDH-impaired cells, indicating a reversal of the malate-aspartate shuttle to synthesize aspartate in SDH/CI impaired cells.
source: However, the observation that GOT1 KO or MDH1 KO prevents CI inhibition from restoring aspartate levels in SDH-impaired cells indicates a reversal of the malate-aspartate shuttle to synthesize aspartate in SDH/CI impaired cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with GOT1 KO and MDH1 KO cells.

claim: Aspartate rescues proliferation of SDH/CI impaired GOT1 KO cells.
source: Finally, we found that the inability of CI inhibition to restore the proliferation of SDH-impaired GOT1 KO cells was due to its lack of aspartate restoration, as aspartate rescues proliferation of SDH/CI impaired GOT1 KO cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In SDH-impaired cells, CI inhibition increases mitochondrial NADH to drive alternative aspartate synthesis pathways via PC and RCQ, both of which yield cytosolic oxaloacetate that is converted to aspartate by GOT1.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that in SDH-impaired cells, CI inhibition increases mitochondrial NADH to drive alternative aspartate synthesis pathways via PC and RCQ, both of which yield cytosolic oxaloacetate that is converted to aspartate by GOT1 (Figure 6I).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with GOT1, GOT2, MDH1, PC, and MPC1 KO cells.

claim: The basal proliferation rate of SDHB KO HEK293T cells progressively increases after several months of passaging.
source: Interestingly, after several months of passaging, we observed that the basal proliferation rate of SDHB KO HEK293T cells progressively increased, and that the proliferation benefit of CI inhibition was lost (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The proliferation benefit of CI inhibition is lost in late passage SDHB KO HEK293T cells.
source: Interestingly, after several months of passaging, we observed that the basal proliferation rate of SDHB KO HEK293T cells progressively increased, and that the proliferation benefit of CI inhibition was lost (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SDHB KO decreases proliferation rate, but culturing SDHB KO cells to late passage allows them to adapt to an improved proliferation rate.
source: We measured proliferation rates of parental cells (WT), AB, EP SDHB KO and LP SDHB KO cells and found that SDHB KO decreased their proliferation rate, but that culturing SDHB KO cells to LP allowed them to adapt to an improved proliferation rate (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Culturing EP SDHB KO cells in the presence of rotenone or aspartate improves cell proliferation.
source: Culturing EP SDHB KO cells in the presence of rotenone or aspartate was able to improve cell proliferation, consistent with the effects of acute SDH inhibition with AA5; however, those benefits were largely lost in LP SDHB KO cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The proliferation benefits of rotenone or aspartate are largely lost in LP SDHB KO cells.
source: Culturing EP SDHB KO cells in the presence of rotenone or aspartate was able to improve cell proliferation, consistent with the effects of acute SDH inhibition with AA5; however, those benefits were largely lost in LP SDHB KO cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Aspartate levels are lowest in EP SDHB KO cells and are increased by either rotenone treatment or by culturing to LP.
source: Consistent with their proliferation rates, aspartate levels were lowest in EP SDHB KO cells and were increased by either rotenone treatment or by culturing to LP (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: EP SDHB KO cells have an increased NAD+/NADH ratio that is diminished upon rotenone treatment.
source: Also similar to the acute effects of AA5 treatment, EP SDHB KO cells had an increased NAD+/NADH ratio that was diminished upon rotenone treatment; however, the NAD+/NADH ratio was already lowered in LP SDHB KO cells and unaffected by rotenone, suggesting redox adaptations occurred during passaging (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The NAD+/NADH ratio is already lowered in LP SDHB KO cells and unaffected by rotenone.
source: Also similar to the acute effects of AA5 treatment, EP SDHB KO cells had an increased NAD+/NADH ratio that was diminished upon rotenone treatment; however, the NAD+/NADH ratio was already lowered in LP SDHB KO cells and unaffected by rotenone, suggesting redox adaptations occurred during passaging (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cells cultured with continuous rotenone treatment remain phenotypically similar to EP cells when CI inhibitors are removed.
source: We found that cells cultured with continuous rotenone treatment remained phenotypically similar to EP cells when CI inhibitors were removed, suggesting the selective pressure is stalled by exogenous CI inhibition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Following complex II proteins, CI proteins are the most statistically significantly different in LP SDHB KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: Comparing WT and LP samples, we conducted MitoPathways 3.0 pathway enrichment analysis (Pagliarini et al., 2008; Rath et al., 2021) of mitochondrial protein abundance changes and found that, following complex II proteins, CI proteins were the most statistically significantly different (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data and GSEA shown in Figure 7E, and citations to Pagliarini et al., 2008 and Rath et al., 2021.

claim: The abundances of most CI subunits are decreased in LP SDHB KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: Indeed, the abundances of most CI subunits were decreased in LP SDHB KO cells compared to WT cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CI subunit levels progressively decrease from WT/AB to EP SDHB KO to LP SDHB KO and result in decreased CI activity.
source: In addition, CI subunit levels progressively decreased from WT/AB to EP SDHB KO to LP SDHB KO and resulted in decreased CI activity, suggesting that SDHB KO cells adapt over time by selecting against CI activity (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 7G and CI activity assay shown in Figure 7H.

claim: SDHB KO cells adapt over time by selecting against CI activity.
source: In addition, CI subunit levels progressively decreased from WT/AB to EP SDHB KO to LP SDHB KO and resulted in decreased CI activity, suggesting that SDHB KO cells adapt over time by selecting against CI activity (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: Inference from proteomics and CI activity data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: LP SDHB KO 143B cells are associated with an ~80% reduction in the CI subunit NDUFA8 compared to WT cells.
source: We confirmed these findings by western blot, where LP SDHB KO 143B cells were associated with an ~80% reduction in the CI subunit NDUFA8 compared to WT cells (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: SDH-deficient cells suppress CI activity to generate an ideal mitochondrial redox state that enables aspartate synthesis.
source: Together, these data suggest that SDH-deficient cells suppress CI activity to generate an ideal mitochondrial redox state that enables aspartate synthesis (Figure 7J).
evidence: Inference from experimental data on CI expression and activity in SDHB KO cells.

claim: UOK269 cells have substantially decreased CI activity compared to WT 143B cells.
source: We thus measured the CI activity of the SDH-null UOK269 cells and found that similar to LP SDHB KO 143B cells, UOK269 cells had substantially decreased CI activity compared to WT 143B cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by CI activity assay shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aspartate is predominantly labeled M+3 from U-13C glucose and U-13C glutamine in WT UOK269 cells.
source: Consistent with the metabolic phenotypes observed in 143B cells, aspartate was predominantly labeled M+3 from U-13C glucose and U-13C glutamine in WT UOK269 cells. SDHB restoration was associated with a loss of glucose-derived aspartate and a restoration of oxidative TCA cycle derived M+4 aspartate from glutamine (Figures Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: SDHB restoration is associated with a loss of glucose-derived aspartate and a restoration of oxidative TCA cycle derived M+4 aspartate from glutamine.
source: Consistent with the metabolic phenotypes observed in 143B cells, aspartate was predominantly labeled M+3 from U-13C glucose and U-13C glutamine in WT UOK269 cells. SDHB restoration was associated with a loss of glucose-derived aspartate and a restoration of oxidative TCA cycle derived M+4 aspartate from glutamine (Figures Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: WT UOK269 cells have minimal NDUFA8 protein expression compared to 143B cells.
source: Consistent with their low CI activity, WT UOK269 cells had minimal NDUFA8 protein expression compared to 143B cells, but interestingly LP SDHB UOK269 cells had restored their NDUFA8 expression (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LP SDHB UOK269 cells have restored NDUFA8 expression.
source: Consistent with their low CI activity, WT UOK269 cells had minimal NDUFA8 protein expression compared to 143B cells, but interestingly LP SDHB UOK269 cells had restored their NDUFA8 expression (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LP SDHB UOK269 cells have substantially increased mitochondrial oxygen consumption and CI activity compared to their SDH-deficient WT counterparts.
source: Correspondingly, LP SDHB UOK269 cells also had substantially increased mitochondrial oxygen consumption and CI activity compared to their SDH-deficient WT counterparts (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 8B and CI activity assay shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The adaptations in CI status are reversible to achieve concordant activity with that of SDH.
source: These results therefore indicate that the adaptations in CI status are reversible to achieve concordant activity with that of SDH.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing CI restoration upon SDHB restoration in UOK269 cells.

claim: DOX treatment of WT UOK269 cells expressing the inducible NDI1 construct results in a substantial induction of mitochondrial oxygen consumption that is resistant to rotenone treatment.
source: DOX treatment of WT UOK269 cells expressing the inducible (iNDI1) construct resulted in a substantial induction of mitochondrial oxygen consumption that was resistant to rotenone treatment, verifying NDI1 expression and confirming that decreased CI activity is a bottleneck for ETC function in UOK269 cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Decreased CI activity is a bottleneck for ETC function in UOK269 cells.
source: DOX treatment of WT UOK269 cells expressing the inducible (iNDI1) construct resulted in a substantial induction of mitochondrial oxygen consumption that was resistant to rotenone treatment, verifying NDI1 expression and confirming that decreased CI activity is a bottleneck for ETC function in UOK269 cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: Inference from oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: NDI1 expression decreases the proliferation of WT UOK269 cells but has no effect on the proliferation of their SDHB-restored counterparts.
source: NDI1 expression decreased the proliferation of WT UOK269 cells but had no effect on the proliferation of their SDHB-restored counterparts (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: NDI1 expression lowers aspartate levels in WT UOK269 cells, but not in the SDHB-restored UOK269 cells.
source: Metabolomics measurements also found that NDI1 expression lowered aspartate levels in WT UOK269 cells, but not in the SDHB-restored UOK269 cells (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: DOX-mediated NDI expression impairs the growth of tumors arising from iNDI1 UOK269 cells.
source: Finally, we tested whether the deleterious effects of CI activity restoration on UOK269 cell proliferation were maintained in a physiological metabolic context by generating mouse xenograft tumors. Notably, DOX-mediated NDI expression also impaired the growth of tumors arising from iNDI1 UOK269 cells (Figure 8G).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Cells adapt to SDH loss by selecting for concordant CI loss, which is required to maximize aspartate production, cell proliferation rate, and tumorigenesis in SDH-null cancer cells.
source: Together, these findings highlight that cells adapt to SDH loss by selecting for concordant CI loss, which is required to maximize aspartate production, cell proliferation rate, and tumorigenesis in SDH-null cancer cells (Figure 8H).
evidence: Inference from experimental data on CI activity, aspartate levels, proliferation, and tumor growth.

claim: Mitochondria play critical roles in cell function beyond efficient ATP synthesis.
source: Central to cell metabolism is the mitochondrion, a double membrane-bound organelle that plays critical roles in cell function. While mitochondria are often viewed through the catabolic lens of efficient ATP synthesis, many proliferating cells can meet their ATP demands from aerobic glycolysis alone yet require intact mitochondrial metabolism for cell proliferation (Weinhouse, 1956; Tan et al., 2015; King and Attardi, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weinhouse, 1956; Tan et al., 2015; King and Attardi, 1989.

claim: Many proliferating cells can meet their ATP demands from aerobic glycolysis alone yet require intact mitochondrial metabolism for cell proliferation.
source: While mitochondria are often viewed through the catabolic lens of efficient ATP synthesis, many proliferating cells can meet their ATP demands from aerobic glycolysis alone yet require intact mitochondrial metabolism for cell proliferation (Weinhouse, 1956; Tan et al., 2015; King and Attardi, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weinhouse, 1956; Tan et al., 2015; King and Attardi, 1989.

claim: The TCA cycle is an amphibolic pathway, serving as both the major catabolic source of mitochondrial NADH and as a primary anabolic route supporting aspartate biosynthesis.
source: The TCA cycle is an amphibolic pathway, serving as both the major catabolic source of mitochondrial NADH and as a primary anabolic route supporting aspartate biosynthesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TCA cycle function.

claim: Supplementation with molecules that regenerate NAD+, such as pyruvate, alpha-ketobutyrate, or duroquinone, can restore the NAD+/NADH ratio and the proliferation of ETC impaired cells.
source: Supplementation with molecules that regenerate NAD+, such as pyruvate, alpha-ketobutyrate, or duroquinone, can restore the NAD+/NADH ratio and the proliferation of ETC impaired cells (Birsoy et al., 2015; Luengo et al., 2021; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Birsoy et al., 2015; Luengo et al., 2021; Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: Heterologous expression of the bacterial NADH oxidase LbNOX can reestablish NADH oxidation independent of the ETC and restore the proliferation of ETC impaired cells.
source: Similarly, heterologous expression of the bacterial NADH oxidase LbNOX can also reestablish NADH oxidation independent of the ETC and restore the proliferation of ETC impaired cells (Titov et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Titov et al., 2016.

claim: Redox regulation is an essential function of ETC activity in proliferating cells.
source: These findings highlight that redox regulation is an essential function of ETC activity in proliferating cells.
evidence: Inference from cited studies on electron acceptors and LbNOX.

claim: A major metabolic consequence of decreased NAD+/NADH upon ETC impairment is depletion of the amino acid aspartate.
source: A major metabolic consequence of decreased NAD+/NADH upon ETC impairment is depletion of the amino acid aspartate (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Birsoy et al., 2015 and Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: Most cells are dependent on de novo aspartate synthesis since aspartate is poorly permeable at physiological concentrations.
source: Most cells are dependent on de novo aspartate synthesis since aspartate is poorly permeable at physiological concentrations (Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2018; Sullivan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2018 and Sullivan et al., 2018.

claim: Aspartate is a central metabolic node in proliferative metabolism, serving as a direct substrate for protein synthesis and as a precursor for the synthesis of other essential metabolites.
source: Aspartate is a central metabolic node in proliferative metabolism, serving as a direct substrate for protein synthesis and as a precursor for the synthesis of other essential metabolites, including asparagine, arginine, and both purine and pyrimidine nucleobases.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of aspartate metabolism.

claim: Providing cells with exogenous sources of aspartate circumvents the proliferative defects of impairments to complexes I, III, and IV without correcting the NAD+/NADH imbalance.
source: Indeed, providing cells with exogenous sources of aspartate circumvents the proliferative defects of impairments to complexes I, III, and IV without correcting the NAD+/NADH imbalance, indicating that ETC impairments block cell proliferation primarily by suppressing aspartate synthesis (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Birsoy et al., 2015 and Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: ETC impairments block cell proliferation primarily by suppressing aspartate synthesis.
source: Indeed, providing cells with exogenous sources of aspartate circumvents the proliferative defects of impairments to complexes I, III, and IV without correcting the NAD+/NADH imbalance, indicating that ETC impairments block cell proliferation primarily by suppressing aspartate synthesis (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference from cited studies and supported by citations to Birsoy et al., 2015 and Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: SDH is a heterotetrameric nuclear-encoded protein complex located in the inner mitochondrial membrane that catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate and shuttles electrons to ubiquinone in the ETC.
source: SDH is a heterotetrameric nuclear-encoded protein complex located in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) that catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate and shuttles electrons to ubiquinone in the ETC.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SDH structure and function.

claim: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations to the subunits of SDH or SDH assembly factors can lead to neoplasms in neuroendocrine tissues and the kidney.
source: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations to the subunits of SDH (A-D) or SDH assembly factors (SDHAF1-2), can lead to neoplasms in neuroendocrine tissues and the kidney (Astuti et al., 2001; Bardella et al., 2011; Baysal et al., 2000; Burnichon et al., 2010; Hao et al., 2009; Niemann and Müller, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Astuti et al., 2001; Bardella et al., 2011; Baysal et al., 2000; Burnichon et al., 2010; Hao et al., 2009; Niemann and Müller, 2000.

claim: Cancer cells arising from mutations in SDH components typically display a complete loss of oxidative TCA cycle metabolism at the SDH step and have a substantial accumulation of the upstream metabolite succinate.
source: Cancer cells arising from mutations in SDH components typically display a complete loss of oxidative TCA cycle metabolism at the SDH step and have a substantial accumulation of the upstream metabolite succinate, which can impair enzymes involved in oxygen sensing, epigenetic regulation, and metabolism (Letouzé et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Letouzé et al., 2013 and Sullivan et al., 2016.

claim: Succinate accumulation can impair enzymes involved in oxygen sensing, epigenetic regulation, and metabolism.
source: Cancer cells arising from mutations in SDH components typically display a complete loss of oxidative TCA cycle metabolism at the SDH step and have a substantial accumulation of the upstream metabolite succinate, which can impair enzymes involved in oxygen sensing, epigenetic regulation, and metabolism (Letouzé et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Letouzé et al., 2013 and Sullivan et al., 2016.

claim: SDH loss blocks the canonical route for aspartate biosynthesis.
source: SDH loss also blocks the canonical route for aspartate biosynthesis, making it unclear how SDH-deficient cells adapt to fulfill their anabolic demands for cell proliferation.
evidence: Inference based on knowledge of TCA cycle and aspartate biosynthesis.
